name: Command pipeline
title: Turn input into arguments.
description: Watch words become batches, placeholders and process argument vectors.
work: Four MyXargs variants read standard input, parse -n/-I/-t/-r, construct commands and use ProcessBuilder. The assignment is a systems-programming foundation for the networking projects.
scope: The archived-behavior view follows the main MyXargs.java tokenization, filtering, batching and empty-input branches. The revised model follows this assignment's convention of replacing a placeholder with all collected input; it is not a complete GNU xargs implementation. No command executes in the browser.
steps: Read standard input into tokens.
Apply the assignment's special-character filter.
Batch tokens or replace a placeholder.
Build an explicit argument list for ProcessBuilder.

name: Threaded chat
title: One listener. Several conversations.
description: Connect virtual clients and follow a message through the server's client-handler registry.
work: TCPClient and TCPServer use port 12345, line-delimited messages, Runnable client handlers, a ConcurrentHashMap registry and independent sender/receiver threads. The server relays to other registered clients and excludes the sender.
scope: This is a deterministic local event model. It opens no sockets and runs no Java threads. The archived model omits join/leave broadcasts as the source does. A revised reference rejects duplicate names and adds notifications. It does not claim to model real scheduling or prove thread safety.
steps: Accept a connection and start a ClientHandler.
Read the username and register the handler.
Read newline-delimited messages.
Relay to peers, then clean up on disconnect.

name: HTTP request desk
title: A request becomes a response.
description: Compare route selection, status codes, MIME types and path handling across two archived server versions and a new reference.
work: The route server handles hello/goodbye text and starts HTTP/optional HTTPS listeners. The static-file variant adds a webroot, MIME mapping, GET/error handling and a canonical-path check. Both use a per-connection Runnable handler.
scope: Only selected behaviors are reconstructed against synthetic fixtures. The model does not serve files, perform TLS, validate certificates or replay every Java parsing edge. The two source variants remain separate; filenames do not prove their chronological or final-submission order.
steps: Accept a connection and read its request line.
Identify the method and target.
Select a fixture or an error status.
Write headers/body and close the connection.

name: Packet observatory
title: Inspect the traffic behind the tools.
description: Explore anonymized headers from every recorded packet, with filters, a timeline and a selected-packet breakdown.
work: The archive includes lab1.pcapng (189 packets) and LAB2.pcapng (11,639 packets). Their enhanced packet blocks were parsed locally into relative timing, endpoint aliases, protocol headers and lengths.
scope: The displayed metadata comes from the supplied captures. No lab worksheet or separate submitted analysis was identified, so no experiment objective or conclusion is invented. Payloads, IP/MAC addresses, DNS names, interface metadata and absolute timestamps are excluded. Port numbers alone do not identify applications.
steps: Choose a capture and protocol filter.
Inspect a packet's relative time and endpoints.
Compare header/payload lengths and TCP flags where available.
Distinguish observation from inferred application behavior.

name: Network calculations
title: Put the numbers on the network.
description: Split an IPv4 address into network/host bits and compare serialization with propagation delay.
work: The course resources cover addressing, protocol layers, transport, routing, link networks, security and performance. This section adds interactive teaching models grounded in that material.
scope: These are new reference exercises, not claimed original submissions. IPv4 host-count conventions distinguish /31 and /32. The delay model assumes one link, propagation speed 2×10^8 m/s, and no queueing or processing delay.
steps: Apply the prefix mask to find the network.
Set host bits to one for the upper address boundary.
Convert packet bytes to bits for transmission time.
Divide distance by propagation speed for travel time.

name: Review & lessons
title: Show what the code actually does.
description: Read strengths, concrete boundary cases and new repairs beside the archived source.
work: The projects show progression from subprocess argument handling to sockets, threaded client handling and HTTP/HTTPS file serving. Source variants, placeholders and companion notes are preserved with their limits.
scope: This review does not reconstruct instructor grades or assert that compilation proves runtime correctness. Native checks cover isolated Java 17 compilation and bounded xargs executions. Browser demos and reviewed repairs are newly created.
steps: Identify the exact source version.
Use a small witness for the behavior in question.
Explain the consequence and a repair.
Keep original evidence separate from the new implementation.

name: Source & references
title: Keep the evidence close.
description: Read all eight Java files, inspect project briefs and browse the complete file inventory.
work: The archive contains three project families, two captures, eight lecture decks, reference books, study guides, notes, editor settings, sample webroot files and bundled setup material.
scope: Only the project PDFs, Java source text, selected notes and anonymized packet metadata enter the site. Keystores, certificates, raw captures, executables and credential-bearing helper commands stay out. Empty CSS/logo placeholders are explicitly recorded.
steps: Read the assignment brief separately from the implementation.
Select the source file and note its public-class name.
Inspect reviewed variants without assuming their chronology.
Use the inventory to locate every original archive file.
